title_original: Dressed to Resist: The Power and Politics of Black Style

blocks.text: From Sunday church attire to contemporary fashion, ‘Sunday Best: The Power & The Glory of Black Style’ at the Art Gallery of Ontario explores how clothing has shaped Black identity, cultural expression and self-determination across generations.
Can getting dressed become a declaration of identity, resistance, and belonging?

In ‘Sunday Best: The Power & The Glory of Black Style ’ , the Art Gallery of Ontario examines the cultural and political significance of fashion within Black diasporic communities, tracing histories of migration, activism and self-expression from the 1880s to the present.

Bringing together fashion, visual art, archival materials and time-based media, the exhibition considers how clothing has served as a powerful language through which Black communities have asserted dignity, celebrated individuality and challenged systems of racial exclusion. At its centre is the enduring tradition of dressing in one’s finest attire, a practice that extends beyond aesthetics to encompass cultural pride, collective memory and the politics of visibility.

Conceived and curated by Dr Julie Crooks and Dr Jason Cyrus, alongside Amanda Bock and Clare Sauro, the exhibition makes its world debut in Toronto. Moving between historical and contemporary expressions of Black style, ‘Sunday Best ’ reveals how fashion operates as both personal expression and collective statement, inviting audiences to reconsider the relationship between appearance, agency and the ongoing struggle for self-representation.
This exhibition is on view at the Art Gallery of Ontario in Toronto until 28 February 2027.
